Preparing Workspace

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

Prompting for Multi-Variable Scatter Plot

```{r}
#Create a ggplot scatter plot using penguins dataset
#Plot bill_length_mm on x-axis and bill_depth_mm on y-axis
#Colour points by species and use geom_point with size = 3
#Add minimal theme and clean labels

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Bill Length vs Bill Depth by Species",
       x = "Bill Length (mm)",
       y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
       color = "Species")

```

Open-Ended Comparative Plotting Distribution check

```{r}

#Generate a boxplot comparing flipper_length_mm across species
#Facet by island
#Use geom_boxplot with fill = species and alpha = 0.7

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ island) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Flipper Length Distribution by Species and Island",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       fill = "Species")
```

Tidyverse Logic

```{r}
#Load tidyverse
library(tidyverse)

#Sample coral data 
coral_monitoring <- tibble(site = c("A", "B", "C"), depth_m = c(12, 35, 8))

#if_else() function is used to classify data based on a condition. It takes three arguments: a logical condition, a value to return if the condition is TRUE, and a value to return if the condition is FALSE.

#Classify depth using if_else ##name of object can be the same to "replace" original
reef_class <- coral_monitoring %>%
  mutate(zone = if_else(depth_m >30, "Deep Reef", "Shallow Reef"))
reef_class

# function mutate()  created new column, modify specified column, or remove column
# %>% is a pipe operator that passes the output of one function to the next function


#case_when() function is used to create new variables based on multiple conditions. It takes a series of logical conditions and corresponding values to return for each condition, 
#It provides a clean, sequential evaluation layout using formula tildes (~) to separate conditions and values.
reef_categories <- coral_monitoring %>%. ##name of object can be the same to "replace" original 
  mutate(reef_category = case_when(
    depth_m < 10 ~ "Lagoon/Reef Flat",
    depth_m <= 30 ~ "Reef Crest/Slope",
    depth_m > 30 ~ "Deep Reef",
    TRUE ~ "Unclassified" #Catch all remainder
  ))

reef_categories

```

Environmental Stress Classification

```{r}

#Generate tibble named "marine_stations" with columns: salinity (35, 28, 32, 12).
#Use pipe operator and mutate combines with case_when() to create new column names "environment_type"
#Classify "environmental_type" by <15 = "Estuarine", 15-30 = "Brackish", >30 = "Marine"

library(tidyverse)

marine_stations <- tibble(salinity = c(35, 28, 32, 12))
environment_classification <- marine_stations %>%
  mutate(environment_type = case_when(
    salinity < 15 ~ "Estuarine",
    salinity >= 15 & salinity <= 30 ~ "Brackish",
    salinity > 30 ~ "Marine",
    TRUE ~ "Unclassified"
  ))
environment_classification

```

Writing Custom Functions

```{r}

#Function Construction Blueprint

#Function Definition
calculate_coral_mortality <- function(initial_count, survival_count) {
  #Logic safety switch using Condition tools
  if(initial_count <= 0){
    stop("Initial count must be greater than zero.")
  }
  mortality_rate <- (initial_count - survival_count) / initial_count
  return(mortality_rate)
}

#Using custom function 
calculate_coral_mortality(initial_count = 120, survival_count = 84)
```

Build a custom function named convert_temp_c_to_f that accepts a single argument representing temperature in Celsius. The function should perform the math conversion: F = (C \* 9/5) + 32. Include a conditional safety check using an if statement that halts execution via stop() if the entered value is below absolute zero (-273.15 degrees Celsius). Test your function with both a valid temperature and an invalid value to ensure the error handling behaves as expected.

```{r}

#Function Definition
convert_temp_c_to_f <- function(celsius) {
  #Logic safety switch using Condition tools
  if(celsius <0){
    stop("Temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15°C).")
  }
  farenhiet <- (celsius * 9/5) + 32
  return(farenhiet)
}

#Using custom function 
convert_temp_c_to_f(celsius = 17) #Expected output: 62.6
convert_temp_c_to_f(celsius = 40) #Expected output: 104
convert_temp_c_to_f(celsius = -10) #Expected output: Error message

```

Advanced Scripting Extension Challenges

Challenge 1: Nested Multi-Vector Iterations In real-world field surveys, calculations often depend on matching values across multiple lists or matrices. Read the documentation for purrr::map2_dbl(). Given a vector of raw survey counts counts \<- c(15, 24, 8, 42) and a vector of species-specific scaling factors factors \<- c(1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 1.1), write a mapping statement that iterates across both vectors simultaneously to return a single vector of scaled abundance values. Do not use a manual index loop.

```{r}

count <- c(15, 24, 8, 42)
scaling_factors <- c(1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 1.1) #species_specific
#Write a mapping statement across both vectors, simultaneously to return a singe vector
#Use map2_dbl() to iterate across both vectors and return a single vector of scaled abundance values
#Note: no manual index loop 

result <- map2_dbl(count, scaling_factors, ~ .x * .y)
result

```

Challenge 2: Robust Data Wrangling Pipeline Function Create a custom function named clean_and_classify_survey that handles complex data frame structures. The function must fulfill these criteria: Accept a data frame and a column name threshold parameter as inputs. Safely check if the specified column name exists within the passed data frame; if it does not, trigger a user-friendly error message using stop(). Filter out rows containing missing values (NA) within that specific column. Use the pipe operator and mutate() along with a vectorised conditional (if_else() or case_when()) to append a status string variable classification based on your threshold parameter. Return the cleaned, altered data frame to the global environment. Test your custom pipeline using a mock tibble that contains at least one missing value to confirm your code handles anomalies without crashing.

```{r}

#Function Definition
#accept data frame and column name as inputs
clean_and_classify_survey <- function(data, site) {
  #Logic safety switch using Condition tools: check if column name exists in the data frame
  #Does not trigger error message if column name is valid
  if_else(!site %in% colnames(data))
    #filter rows containing NAs
    na.omit_data <- data %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[site]]))
    #mutate and vectorised conditional (if_else()) or case_when() to append a status string variable classification based on the values in the specified column
    mutate_data <- na.omit_data %>%
      mutate(classification = case_when(
        .data[[site]] < 10 ~ "Low",
        .data[[site]] >= 10 & .data[[site]] <= 20 ~ "Medium",
        .data[[site]] > 20 ~ "High",
        TRUE ~ "Unclassified"
      ))
      return(mutate_data) #Return the cleaned, altered data frame to the global environment
}
  
data <- tibble(
  site = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  count = c(5, 15, NA, 25)
)

```

Working Code

```{r}
library(dplyr)

clean_and_classify_survey <- function(data, site) {
  # Logic safety switch: check if column name exists in the data frame
  if (!site %in% colnames(data)) {
    stop(paste("Error: Column", site, "does not exist in the data frame."))
  }
  
  # Filter rows containing NAs in the specified column
  na.omit_data <- data %>% 
    filter(!is.na(.data[[site]]))
  
  # Append a status string variable classification based on the values
  mutate_data <- na.omit_data %>%
    mutate(classification = case_when(
      .data[[site]] < 10 ~ "Low",
      .data[[site]] >= 10 & .data[[site]] <= 20 ~ "Medium",
      .data[[site]] > 20 ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified"
    ))
  
  return(mutate_data) 
}

# Create the test data frame
data <- tibble(
  site = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  count = c(5, 15, NA, 25)
)

# Run the function using "count" as the column target
cleaned_data <- clean_and_classify_survey(data, "count")
print(cleaned_data)

```
